    Breaking: Podcast Episode 762: Off-Site Construction, Quiet Roof Assemblies, and a Fix for Attic AC

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1336 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, welcome to the Fine Homebuilding Podcast, our weekly discussion of building, remodeling, and design topics aimed at anybody who cares deeply about the craft and science of working on houses.
    • Sources indicate that please email us your questions to [email protected].
    • It’s been getting cold at night around here.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, welcome to the Fine Homebuilding Podcast, our weekly discussion of building, remodeling, and design topics aimed at anybody who cares deeply about the craft and science of working on houses. In this episode, Ian and Randy help Patrick address listener feedback and answer their questions. Kevin shares a Boston Globe opinion piece on manufactured housing as a way to build more houses. Keith asks about using mineral wool insulation to help control sound in an expansive space. Rob considers building an insulated box around his attic air handler to boost its efficiency.

    Sources indicate that please email us your questions to [email protected]. You can find previous podcasts and check out the show notes at finehomebuilding.com/podcast.

    Ian: I hope you’re done painting. It’s been getting cold at night around here.

    Randy: Is your furnace and ductwork all done?

    Patrick: Tool test of cordless oscillating multitools by Aaron Miiller.

    In a recent development, off-site construction is a subject that needs more attention in the US. I’m glad that Tedd Benson keeps getting good press.

    Industry observers note that kevin sent us a Boston Globe editorial piece describing why Massachusetts needs more modular or manufactured housing. It mentions Bensonwood and quotes Mark Hetzlera, a Bensonwood employee. It’s an editorial, not a reported piece, so it shouldn’t be held to the same standards as journalism. Editorials represent the views of the Boston Globe Editorial Board.

    Make it Easier to Build More Modular Housing.

    I’m an owner-builder in Bay City, Oregon, in Marine Climate Zone 4C. I’m planning a single-slope roof with a 3:12 pitch and a 24-ft. clear span using parallel-chord trusses. My assembly plan consists of standing-seam aluminum roofing over purlins, 4 in. of continuous polyiso, taped Zip sheathing as the primary air barrier, and a truss cavity filled with 8 in. of mineral wool or fiberglass batts, for a target total insulation value of R-56. The interior will be acoustic fabric (a black muslin theater fabric) and then wood slats with gaps to form an acoustic ceiling. I’m not planning for an interior membrane planned so the acoustic function works as designed.

    My question is: With 4 in. of exterior polyiso and Zip sheathing serving as the primary air barrier, what building science function would an additional interior air or vapor-control layer serve? Would an acoustically open ceiling be compatible with this assembly, or am I missing a key risk? If so, do you have any ideas how I might make this work?

    Thanks for all you do. I appreciate any guidance and absolutely LOVE the show!

    It has been revealed that one last thing: As a former radio host, I appreciate good voices, and Ian’s is so distinctive and awesome! It reminds me of Patrick Warburton, the actor who voices Officer Joe Swanson on Family Guy.

    As a fellow Oregonian, I know the 4C climate zone well. In a lot of ways, its a Goldilocks zone—not too humid, not too dry. The climate tends to be pretty forgiving, with the exception of our frequent rains.

    As I evaluate assemblies, I always define and break out the control layers to see if there are any challenges. Beyond water, air, vapor, and thermal, it is good to consider wind and fire control layers. The most glaring omission I see is a well-defined water control layer. I consider roofing to be a water-shedding layer, as water can get through via penetrations, mistakes, etc. You blueprint to use polyiso, but you didn’t specify the facer type. In our area, the most commonly used facer in the roofing community is fiberglass faced, but aluminum facer is easily sourced, too. The former would make a terrible water control layer and the latter would be okay, except you would have to tape all the seams, and aluminum isn’t the most durable. I would start by installing a self-adhered WRB or roof underlayment directly on top of the polyiso. The permeability doesn’t really matter (more on that to come). This would be your primary bulk-water control layer. The next most key layer is the air control layer. As long as you tape the seams of the Zip sheathing, you should be good there. Pay attention to how  the roof air barrier connects to the wall air barrier to maintain continuity.

    For vapor control, of all the materials in this assembly, foil-faced polyiso would be the least permeable, as it is a Class 1 vapor barrier. If the polyiso is fiberglass-faced, it is a Class 3 semi-permeable vapor retarder, with a permeance of roughly 1 to 4 perms. The OSB in the Zip is roughly the same at 3 perms. In one sense, vapor control becomes less of a concern because you have created a vented assembly with the purlins below the metal roofing. In another sense, it may be a moot point because the thickness of the insulation should keep the Zip sheathing warm enough to prevent condensation. At approximately R-20, the exterior insulation would also meet the code requirement in our area. If vapor were to pass through, it would simply get whisked away via the vented gap. If you were to put a vapor-closed roof underlayment on top of the fiberglass-faced polyiso, the combination would essentially a layer similar to foil facing. In both cases, you are fine because the insulation is thick enough to keep condensation from forming on the bottom side of the Zip. If anything, a vapor-open membrane would be slightly more resilient, but we are splitting hairs in the weeds at this point.

    It has been revealed that for the thermal control layer, the main change I would make is to switch to two layers of 2-in. polyiso boards in lieu of one 4-in. layer. Rigid insulation is prone to shrink, and by offsetting the seams you will avoid numerous thermal breaks throughout the assembly. On the interior, pick whichever fluffy insulation you like. Eight inches should work well, but adding a few more Rs wouldn’t hurt, either. From a wind-washing control perspective, mineral wool and wood fiber are denser than fiberglass, so I would consider those. One wants to avoid the thermal degradation from wind washing– think about a sweater on a windy day.

    It has been revealed that patrick’s point about the fire control is valid. If you were to install a layer of Sheetrock and fire-tape it, its vapor-open nature means it wouldn’t affect the assembly at all. From a sound-control perspective, you might consider applying an elastomeric acoustic sealant and/or installing resilient channels before hanging the Sheetrock. From that point, adding the black muslin fabric and wood slats would work well.

    According to recent reports, I’m reaching out for some guidance. Earlier this summer during a storm, we lost a large tree in front of our house. It turns out that a good afternoon shade tree can cover up a few building science sins. In the 19 years we’ve lived here, we’ve gotten by with our AC air handler in the unconditioned attic. But without that tree blocking much of the afternoon and setting sun, the AC has clearly been working harder this summer, making it obvious that more than a new tree is needed.

    I realize step one is getting a proper energy audit, but in the meantime I have a few questions:.

    Sorry for the length of the letter, but I feel like this has all snowballed on me and could really use your help getting this project organized.

    Sources indicate that thanks to Randy, Ian, and Cari for joining me and thanks to all of you for listening. Remember to send us your questions and suggestions to [email protected] and please like, comment, or review us no matter how you’re listening–it helps other folks find our podcast.

    #32472. How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1045 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finegardening ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that people often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan.
    • I like to create purpose-driven designs.
    • Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that people often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan. While every client and garden is different, I usually start with the same basic questions.

    I like to create purpose-driven designs. For example, I’m often called on to solve a problem, even if it is simply “I have a new house and a blank slate.” It may be just a section of the garden, the front yard, or something specific like repairing a garden after a new septic system installation or after a new house is built next door.

    Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light. Questions help people consider things they would not normally think about. As a result, these conversations define their needs and desires, helping me combine different elements into a cohesive design.

    The same approach applies to projects in my own garden. I don’t give myself a questionnaire, but I do ask myself the same questions. First, I assess the challenges, the location of the area in relation to the rest of the property, and the environmental conditions that will influence the planting.

    According to recent reports, in a upcoming garden, the major goal is often screening. Most people want privacy to live their lives outside without having to see a neighboring house, road, commercial area, or vacant lot.

    In a recent development, privacy was one of the substantial considerations when planning my grass garden. There was no privacy between my property and the neighboring property. I could see my neighbors eat their dinner, watch them play with their grandchildren, and even see them argue. Their house was also too close to the property line, and in fact, their sidewalk was on my property. That was a problem.

    Because the sidewalk was already there when I moved in, I had to incorporate it into my design, but I could still make it disappear visually.

    Sources indicate that I started out with some tall elements at the back of the bed to start the screening process. I positioned these plants so I could maintain them from my property without having branches extend over the property line. Keeping their mature size in mind also helped avoid potential conflicts with the neighboring property. Soft screens made of trees and tall shrubs (both evergreen and deciduous) offer privacy without creating a harsh, artificial boundary line.

    Read More: 20 Unique Hedging Plant Options.

    Looking at the space, I could see a definite focal point within my property. With the neighbor behind me, the view naturally led the eye toward the water. Therefore, I designed a one-sided border rather than an island bed meant to be viewed from multiple directions. Making the border as deep as 20 feet in places gave me enough room to continue screening the neighboring property while also providing some sound buffering.

    Recent findings suggest that understanding the environmental conditions was the next step. The back edge is on the north side of my property. The large trees and shrubs would not shade the rest of the bed. This meant the bed would be in full sun all day, all season long.

    What a challenge for this PNW native who grew up mostly in the forest (or woods, as we called it). I had to learn about plants that liked full sun, drying winds, and dry soil so they could thrive. Rather than trying to re-create the shaded woodland conditions I knew best, I needed to work with what the site naturally offered.

    Read More: Summer-Dry Gardening: A Visit to Beth Chatto’s Gravel Garden.

    In a recent development, growing up in the forest, I longed for wide-open sky and long views. Above all, I wanted to immerse myself in the garden. A long row of hedging plants that I could only look at wasn’t what I had in mind. I wanted to become part of the blowing, rustling movement of the grasses. While experiencing the plants, I also wanted to connect with insects, pollinators, birds, frogs, and even a few rabbits.

    In a recent development, I consider the challenge met. The amount of wildlife activity surrounding me in the garden never ceases to amaze me. I feel as if I’m in a different world while surrounded by all the action and movement of the grasses and perennials, far away from big cedar trees, moss, and ferns. Sun, wind, fragrant flowers, and the smell of warm earth are all-encompassing there.

    Even during the winter, this garden pulls me out, bundled up and coffee in hand, to see what is happening. Early spring bulbs push through the soil, mice shelter under the evergreen sedges, and birds search for a breakfast of grass seeds and gather bits and pieces to build new nests.

    It has been revealed that the ultimate goal of any designer is finding the right outdoor elements to pull people outside and connect them with nature. Those elements are individual to each client. They could be an eating area, outdoor kitchen, hot tub, play area, pond, fountain, or hidden sitting area. Maybe the goal is plant-driven, with a vegetable garden, cutting garden, or collection of conifers.

    When these features are thoughtfully integrated with immersive, naturalistic plantings, the result is an outdoor space that invites people to experience their gardens throughout the year.

    Discuss this article or ask gardening questions with a regional gardening expert on the Gardening Answers forum.

    And for more Pacific Northwest regional reports, click here.

    Susan Calhoun is the owner and principal designer of Plantswoman Design in Bainbridge Island, Washington.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, hi GPOD! I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD. Unfortunately, I haven’t received any submissions through the form in quite a while. I’m not sure what the problem is, but hopefully there will be a resolution soon. In the meantime, you can submit your photos and captions through the email linked below instead.

    According to recent reports, today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota. And while looking through their latest photos, I kept forgetting that I was looking at a garden in the Midwest! Arianne has shared their garden with us before, and I’m excited to see what they’ve been growing this year. Here’s Arianne:.

    Industry observers note that in Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden! It’s packed with flowers I start from seed—like zinnias, cosmos, statice, strawflower, celosia, and amaranth—along with overwintered dahlias. I love cutting fresh bouquets to gift to friends, family, and coworkers. When we’re not admiring the blooms, my husband is cooking outdoors—making wood-fired pizzas, wok dishes, and hosting family birthday celebrations right in the heart of our cozy yard.

    Sources indicate that arianne packs plenty of interest into the garden along in the front yard and along the curb strip. Plants in this section of the garden include dwarf purple smokebush, threadleaf bluestar (Amsonia hubrichtii, Zones 5–8), boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), lamb’s ear (Stachys byzantina, Zones 4–8), purpleleaf sand cherry (Prunus × cistena, Zones 2–8), coreopsis (Coreopsis cvs., Zones 3–9), alliums (Allium cvs., Zones 3–9), sedum, and artemisia. It’s a great mix of foliage colors and textures even when everything isn’t in bloom.

    It has been revealed that I love the placement of the patio and pathway. It’s a really useful design technique for maximizing every square inch of a small garden while still leaving plenty of room for outdoor living.

    Absolutely gorgeous section of the garden! This is where we really start to feel like we’re in the tropics. ‘Mars Madness’ hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus ‘Mars Madness’, Zones 4–9) has all the tropical drama while still being hardy enough for a Minneapolis winter. And it’s hard to miss those giant cannas and the colorful foliage on the coleus. I love all the red blooms too!

    Industry observers note that one of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual). So much of the color and interest here comes from foliage!

    There is so much to look at in this section of the garden! Those variegated geranium leaves are striking, and I could go on and on about Arianne’s use of color and texture. The apple tree surrounded by all these ornamentals is an unexpected but lovely touch.

    It has been revealed that just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

    Industry observers note that another view of the backyard borders. There are so many plants packed into this garden, you would never believe this is a small urban backyard. And, if my eyes are working correctly, I’d say that’s a clover lawn?!

    Tall conifers create a fantastic privacy screen in this view. The garden really is its own secluded paradise.

    A shady combination of hostas, ‘Banana Boat’ sedge (Carex siderosticha ‘Banana Boat’, Zones 4–9), painted fern, purple shield, coleus, and impatiens.

    Recent findings suggest that zinnias, statice, amaranth, and overwintered dahlias are just some of the blooms that make their way into bouquets for friends, family, and coworkers. So pretty!

    Sources indicate that thank you so much for sharing your garden with us again, Arianne! It’s always a treat to see what you and Micah are growing, and I think I could spend hours wandering around this garden and still find something new to admire.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Department of Justice and FBI declared today results of the personnel surge in support of Operation Not Forgotten 2026, which focuses on unresolved cases in Indian country with a priority on cases involving violence against women and children, including those who are missing or murdered.

    In its fourth year, Operation Not Forgotten surged personnel and investigative resources across the country from April 1 through September 30, resulting in 118 arrests, 41 individuals charged federally, 25 child victims identified or located, and 72 weapons recovered. FBI agents conducted 990 interviews and 232 search operations. Arrests increased by 123% and subjects charged by 52% over 2025.

    “The Department of Justice will always work to deliver justice for the victims of violent crime in Indian country,” stated Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the hard work of the FBI, our U.S. Attorneys, and other federal and tribal partners, Operation Not Forgotten and Operation Steadfast Promise are helping make communities safer and providing comfort for victims and families.”.

    According to recent reports, “This year’s Operation Not Forgotten continued this FBI’s largest commitment to Indian Country in the history of the Bureau,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “The results were outstanding – from April 1 through September 30, this FBI worked more than 500 cases, a 59% increase from last year’s operation; 118 arrests, a 123% increase; and 41 subjects charged federally, a 52% increase. This is in addition to 25 child victims identified or located and 72 weapons recovered. These involved life-saving operations, with cases including child sexual abuse, physical assault and abuse, domestic violence, CSAM cases, and more.

    Sources indicate that “Operation Not Forgotten sends a loud and clear message that our long-forgotten partners in Indian Country are forgotten no more,” mentioned Director Patel. “When I assumed the position of FBI Director a year and a half ago, this FBI promised we would be there for our tribal partners. We have and will continue to be – through our 400 agents dedicated to Indian country, 30 Safe Trails Task Forces, and increased awareness with our Voices Not Forgotten program, where the FBI quadrupled the rewards to at least $25,000 for information associated with homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country. Thank you to our federal, state, and local partners who continue to work with us to ensure these unsolved crimes and cases receive the surge in resources they deserve.”.

    It has been revealed that “Operation Not Forgotten demonstrates the Trump Administration’s commitment to protecting tribal communities, strengthening public safety, and ensuring that victims and their families have access to justice,” stated Billy Kirkland, Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs, U.S. Department of the Interior. “Through close collaboration across the federal government and in partnership with tribal, state, and local law enforcement, we are bringing additional resources and investigative support to Indian Country to address violent crime, advance unresolved cases, and help families find answers. The Department of the Interior, through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, remains committed to working alongside our partners to deliver meaningful results and build safer communities for generations to come.".

    Examples of cases charged during this period include:.

    Recent findings suggest that in the District of Wyoming, the surge resulted in the federal indictment of 18 individuals for an array of violent crimes, and child abuse offenses on the Wind River Indian Reservation, including U.S. v. Jose Benito Ocon: This prosecution arises from an August 2025 incident near Riverton, where the defendant allegedly executed a male passenger with a gunshot to the head inside a moving vehicle before turning the firearm on two female witnesses.     Maryland Man Convicted of $18.7 Million Medicare Fraud for Respiratory Testing Scheme Targeting Nursing Homes

    📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (798 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A federal jury in the District of Maryland convicted a laboratory owner yesterday for taking advantage of nursing homes that needed COVID-19 tests during the pandemic and fraudulently billing Medicare more than $18 million for other expensive respiratory tests that nursing home residents did not need, physicians did not order, and, in many cases, were never performed.
    • Britton-Harr’s decision to exploit elderly nursing‑home residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable.
    • It has been revealed that “This verdict sends a clear message: the FBI will aggressively pursue anyone who steals from American taxpayers,” remarked FBI Baltimore Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A federal jury in the District of Maryland convicted a laboratory owner yesterday for taking advantage of nursing homes that needed COVID-19 tests during the pandemic and fraudulently billing Medicare more than $18 million for other expensive respiratory tests that nursing home residents did not need, physicians did not order, and, in many cases, were never performed.

    “Mr. Britton-Harr’s decision to exploit elderly nursing‑home residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable. This verdict reinforces our message: there is nowhere to hide for those who commit fraud. We will find you and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law,” said U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes for the District of Maryland. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office, along with our law-enforcement partners, remains committed to rooting out fraud and holding accountable those who exploit our vulnerable victims and who steal our taxpayer money.”.

    It has been revealed that “This verdict sends a clear message: the FBI will aggressively pursue anyone who steals from American taxpayers,” remarked FBI Baltimore Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul. “Patrick Britton-Harr will now face the consequences of his greed and brazen crimes. In addition to this healthcare fraud scheme, Britton-Harr was previously convicted for investment fraud in which the FBI uncovered a separate scheme where he defrauded private citizens. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will not rest until fraudsters like Mr. Britton Harr are brought to justice.”.

    According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Patrick Britton-Harr, 42, of Annapolis, offered COVID-19 tests to nursing homes across the country in 2020 when these facilities were desperate for COVID-19 testing services. After specimens were collected from nursing home residents and other laboratories performed COVID-19 testing, Britton-Harr billed Medicare for separate, high-priced respiratory pathogen panel (RPP) tests purportedly conducted in a laboratory he owned in Arizona. Britton-Harr falsely claimed to Medicare that treating physicians ordered these extensive RPP tests, which screened for more than 30 respiratory pathogens. In reality, physicians never ordered the tests for their nursing home patients, and several physicians testified at trial they had never ordered an RPP test for any patient during the entirety of their medical careers.

    Recent findings suggest that through his company, Provista Health, Britton-Harr fraudulently billed Medicare $18.7 million for RPP testing purportedly performed in just six months, of which Medicare paid more than $7.2 million. Evidence at trial demonstrated how Britton-Harr exploited inexperienced employees, including a family member and high school and college aged interns, by directing them to bill Medicare for an RPP test every time a COVID-19 test was performed. Britton-Harr further directed the billing of RPP tests supposedly performed at his Arizona laboratory after he had already closed the laboratory, barred staff from working in the laboratory, and no longer had the equipment necessary to run RPP tests. Additional evidence at trial proved that Britton-Harr billed Medicare for RPP tests that were never performed, including billing for tests for nursing home residents who were already deceased.

    Britton-Harr used the proceeds of his fraud scheme to fund a lavish lifestyle, purchasing, among other things, a $112,500 Porsche 911, and making $25,000 monthly mortgage payments on his Annapolis waterfront mansion.

    Recent findings suggest that the jury convicted Britton-Harr of five counts of health care fraud and one count of transactional money laundering. Britton-Harr faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison for each count. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled at a later date. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

    HHS-OIG and FBI investigated the case.

    Trial Attorney Chris Wenger of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Ari Evans for the District of Maryland are prosecuting the case.

    It has been revealed that on April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

    Industry observers note that the Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, presently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.

    In a recent development, when evaluating these hydroponic home garden systems, we considered over a dozen companies and looked at the brand, customer reviews, features of the product, extra items included, and how well the system grew plants.     In a recent development, we scored each product using a rubric that evaluated the watering system, how well the plants in the system thrived, how easy the system was to set up and use, any extra features the product included, types of plants the system could grow, the durability of the product, and how attractive the setup was. We also considered the cost value of each product.

    As we tested each hydroponic system, we looked closely at how well the plants grew and how easy the system was to use and maintain. To do this, we tested each system for a minimum of a month, and some of the systems were tested for over a year.

    Plants need four essential elements to thrive: water, oxygen, light, and nutrients. A successful hydroponic system must supply an adequate amount of all four. For those new to cultivating an indoor garden, the options may seem confusing, but today’s manufacturers offer various types of hydroponic systems that automate much of the process.

    While all hydroponic systems supply plant roots with water and nutrients, the method varies. There are six common types of hydroponic systems, all with unique strong points, but some are better suited to commercial settings than DIY home settings.

    Hydroponic gardening at home is not difficult, but the operator will need basic knowledge about how hydroponics work. This means, for most systems, that growers should have some experience in sprouting plants from seeds, knowing when plants need plant food, monitoring the water flow of the reservoir, and adjusting nutrient levels and pH.

    Fortunately, with today’s consumer hydroponic systems, indoor gardening is simple and straightforward. Systems like the popular AeroGarden come with mesh pods and soilless medium (often coconut coir plugs), as well as a pump for circulating water and keeping roots moist and healthy. Unlike classic terrariums, most of today’s in-home systems also feature grow lights on timers that provide the correct amount of light for optimal growth.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the convenient characteristics of a hydroponic grow system is that users can grow more plants in less space because the roots don’t need to spread out to seek nutrients. Depending on the type of setup, hydroponic systems can be as small as a few inches deep by a few inches wide or as massive as a few feet deep by a few feet wide. The most common models, such as the AeroGarden Harvest, can fit on a kitchen countertop, ladder plant stand, or a table and take up no more than 1 to 2 square feet of space—yet some models can grow up to 30 full-size plants.

    It has been revealed that indoor hydroponic systems can grow a wide variety of plant types. While smaller systems, such as the AeroGarden, are best used for herbs and smaller varieties of peppers and tomatoes, larger systems like the Lettuce Grow Farmstand can grow virtually anything, including large lettuces, full-size tomato or pepper plants, kale, Swiss chard, bok choy, and even cabbage. Flowers can be grown in hydroponic systems, too.

    Consistent temperature is essential to plant growth, so commercial hydroponic growers often have water heaters to regulate the water temperature. However, in-home hydroponic systems don’t require the same temperature-control level because they’re usually placed in a home where the temperature remains between 60 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit. Many experts suggest that the optimal water temperature for plant growth is between 68 and 71.6 degrees Fahrenheit.

    According to recent reports, unlike self-watering planter systems, a soilless growing medium is normally used in hydroponic gardening. These mediums can include coconut coir plugs or mineral wool. However, some systems, such as the Lettuce Grow Farmstand, have plants that are started in actual soil and then transplanted into small pods to grow without additional soil in the hydroponic system.

    Some systems come with plants or seeds already in the substrate. As the plants grow, the roots extend below the pod into the reservoir or channel beneath.

    Recent findings suggest that nutrients used in hydroponic systems can be in either powder or liquid form. Some come with powders that must be dissolved in warm water before being added to the water reservoir, while other systems come with liquid plant food that can be poured directly into the reservoir.

    In a recent development, automated hydroponic systems require minimal maintenance relative to a traditional garden or a DIY hydroponics system. Most systems recommend topping off the tank reservoir about once a week and adding plant food at the same time. It’s also recommended that the reservoir be cleaned every month or so to prevent the buildup of algae in the tank.

    During the growing cycle, users may also need to wipe down the unit’s surface with a clean, damp rag to maintain its appearance—they aren’t immune to dust!

    There are many advantages to owning a hydroponic grow kit, including water conservation, reduced risk of pest problems, and fresh produce year-round.

    According to recent reports, according to Dr. Michael B. Timmons, professor emeritus and graduate professor in the Department of Biological and Environmental Engineering at Cornell University, “Producing food as efficiently as possible and minimizing the use of our scarce resources should be a goal for everyone. Each family could contribute toward this goal by choosing to produce some or all of the vegetables they eat. Producing vegetables hydroponically using controlled environment agriculture (CEA) … uses 90 percent less water and land than conventional agriculture.” He goes on to say that those who grow some of their food hydroponically can reduce the associated carbon footprint by producing in their own home, garage, or mini-greenhouse.

    Industry observers note that as explained by the Oklahoma State University Extension, one of the advantages of utilizing a hydroponic system to grow vegetables and flowers is being able to control the nutrients and growing environment. Hydroponic systems also reduce the risk of chemical exposure due to pesticides as well as the risk of pests infesting the plants and soil (although the plants are not immune to pests that may travel indoors). Finally, with an all-inclusive hydroponic system, growing herbs, fruits, veggies, or flowers indoors needn’t take a lot of time or require a large garden or a sunny window.

    Because hydroponic systems automate the growing process, users don’t need a lot of gardening or hydroponic knowledge to enjoy fresh herbs and produce. For those upcoming to growing indoors, however, some questions are to be expected. Read on for answers that provide basic info.

    For those just developing a green thumb, an affordable hydroponics system that automates lighting and watering and provides a few growing stations is ideal.

    Most systems come with built-in aeration via a pump, so additional aeration is not needed.

    No. Nutrient solutions are preformulated to offer the best pH level for a wide variety of plants and herbs. However, you may want to test the pH level of the water in the reservoir with a pH test kit and add pH-adjusting liquid to raise or lower the pH level to about 6 or 7, which is the ideal range for growing vegetables and herbs.

    Recent findings suggest that to maintain a strict pH level, pH-adjusting liquids are available, and a couple of drops of either “pH Up” or “pH Down” can change the level. Some hydroponic systems come with a testing kit, but these are often a separate purchase.

    Sources indicate that yes. Each indoor growing system has its own recommendations on how often to clean it, and some systems recommend cleaning as often as once a month. In general, cleaning requires removing all the spent plants and scrubbing or wiping out the unit—especially the water reservoir—before using it again. Apart from that, wipe down the surfaces with a clean, damp rag as necessary to remove dust, plant debris, and grime.

    Sources indicate that to choose the right lineup of lunch boxes for the varying needs of construction workers, we considered the amount of food and drink each option could carry as well as the holding temperatures they could maintain to keep consumable items safe and fresh. Though we were also careful about selecting options to fit a range of budgets, we ruled out cheaply made, low-quality lunch boxes in favor of products that offer lasting value for long-term use.

For Jay, “a tight-fitting lid that keeps food at the desired temperature for hours” and “chemical-free lunch boxes for meals that don’t harm your health” are the most important considerations.

    Since lunch boxes designed for the office or coolers for the beach may not stand up to the rigors of the jobsite, evaluating construction worker lunch boxes based on the following key elements will ensure you get the right product for your needs.

    It has been revealed that lunch boxes aren’t always treated with the greatest care. Those that have a tough outer shell will be more resistant to damage from the knocks and bumps that are part of life on a busy construction site. Hard-sided lunch boxes can help prevent food from getting smashed, and some are even strong enough to sit on while you eat. Though they are more durable, their construction can make them a bit heavier, bulkier, and less portable.

    On the other hand, soft-sided and collapsible coolers are quite portable. They’re almost always lighter than hard models, are a snap to store, and are frequently less expensive. Though soft-sided coolers don’t provide as much protection for their contents as hard options, a soft lunch box can be a perfectly viable option if your lunch will wait in a vehicle rather than be toted directly to the site.

    Recent findings suggest that capacity requirements largely depend on how substantial a meal you typically pack. A larger capacity may be more versatile—it can be used for a family weekend outing, for example. Conversely, the best small coolers will be sized just right for single-meal use as well as more portable and easier to store.

    Sources indicate that capacity descriptions vary. Often, they are given as a number of standard beverage cans, making capacity fairly easy to visualize. Quart capacity is another common measurement. Those given in inches can make it difficult to picture the true size, so it may be smart to fold some cardboard into roughly the measurements given to avoid ordering a lunch box that’s too small or large.

    Multiple compartments (as often found in bento boxes) are convenient for those who take various items for lunch and wish to keep them separated. One of our top picks even includes a pill organizer.

    A well-insulated construction lunch box can keep food cool or warm for some time. However, while some manufacturers indicate how long they expect the contents to maintain temperature, their estimates may be optimistic, and there isn’t any recognized standard for the amount of insulation a lunch box or cooler provides. Shoppers should use their best judgment: Look at the thickness of the insulation, how rugged the fabric and seams are, and how well the insulated area closes.

    Sources indicate that how a construction worker lunch box is carried and how easily it opens and closes is also worth considering, so examine the soundness of handles and clasps. Those likely to pack ice in the lunch box should also check how leakproof it is, particularly with soft cool boxes.

    All aspects of jobsite safety are important—even regarding your lunch box. Certain products previously used to produce plastics are now deemed unsafe for use with food. The organic compound bisphenol A (known as BPA) is one of the main culprits, though PVC and phthalates (which make plastics more flexible) should also be avoided. Many manufacturers will state whether their plastic containers are free of these materials. Since food hygiene is a crucial part of food safety, remember also to consider how easy it will be to thoroughly wash all areas of the container.

    The guide above contains useful information and vetted products to help you choose the best lunch box for construction workers. Anyone with additional questions about how to choose and use a rugged, reliable lunch box will find more information below.

    As with the best coolers, keeping lunch cold in a lunch box is best accomplished by using an insulated ice bag or box with ice blocks or bags of ice inside.

    It has been revealed that the body can absorb aluminum through contact with food. However, many sources say it passes through naturally and does not present health problems. Some aluminum lunch boxes are specifically marked as food safe.

    The best way to clean most lunch boxes is with a sponge and warm, soapy water, though the manufacturer may have its own suggestions, and these should take priority.

    Health experts often suggest you replace your lunch box every year since even the best options can accumulate small amounts of mold and bacteria in hard-to-clean crevices. If damaged, a lunch box should be replaced immediately to prevent any risk of contamination.

    Generally speaking, no, lunch boxes are not microwavable. If you need a microwavable container, consider packing something like these PrepNaturals glass meal-prep containers inside your lunch box.

    3 Winterization Projects That Are as Easy as Painting

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
    • Industry observers note that winter weather can be devastating to outdoor furniture, appliances, and structures, which is why many people store as much as possible in a covered shed or garage throughout the cold season.
    • Outdoor winterization projects that involve painting, staining, or sealing help surfaces create a durable barrier against freeze-thaw cycles, moisture intrusion, and corrosive deicing salts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    Industry observers note that winter weather can be devastating to outdoor furniture, appliances, and structures, which is why many people store as much as possible in a covered shed or garage throughout the cold season. Even though not everything can be neatly tucked away, such as your deck, walkways, and gates, you can take steps to prepare them for harsh winter conditions before snow starts to fall.

    Outdoor winterization projects that involve painting, staining, or sealing help surfaces create a durable barrier against freeze-thaw cycles, moisture intrusion, and corrosive deicing salts. It’s key to complete these protective jobs before the first hard freeze so you can prevent deep structural damage during the winter months.

    Leaving wood decks, fences, or patio furniture bare during winter allows moisture from snow and ice to seep into the wood pores. When trapped water freezes, it expands, causing the wood to split, warp, and rot. A fresh coat of waterproof sealant or oil-based stain acts as a hydrophobic barrier. Water pools on top of the sealed surface rather than penetrating the wood grain.

    Industry observers note that before applying a compatible exterior stain or water-repellent finish, clean the surface, remove failing finish, and allow the wood to dry sufficiently. For decking and steps, choose a winterization product specifically approved for horizontal surfaces and foot traffic.

    Marc Sharkey, owner of Dynamic Painting Inc, indicates that “the finish reduces water absorption from rain and melting snow. Repeated wetting and drying can contribute to checking, splitting, and warping; prolonged dampness also creates conditions for decay.

    “Pay particular attention to exposed board ends and areas where the old finish has worn away.” He also warns: “A latest coating cannot repair rotten wood.” Given that Sharkey’s business is based in Alberta, he has experience dealing with some of the harshest winters in North America.

    This oil-based formula provides corrosion resistance and weather protection for outdoor metal surfaces . Learn more in our buyer’s guide.

    Winter preparation is important to safeguard your home. Chipped paint on steel or iron railings, furniture, and gates exposes the raw metal to oxygen and winter humidity, rapidly accelerating the oxidation process. Road salt or salt-based sidewalk ice melts further expedite this corrosion, eating through the metal structures. Applying a coat of exterior, rust-resistant enamel or oil-based paint seals out moisture and oxygen, halting the chemical reaction that creates rust.

    It’s a budget-friendly winterization project that also forms a slick, chemical-resistant barrier against salt splash-back. Before applying a coating, remove loose rust and flaking paint and clean away dirt and salt. Then apply an appropriate rust-inhibiting primer and exterior metal finish. Check compatibility carefully: steel, aluminum, and galvanized metal can require different preparation and primers.

    “An intact coating limits exposure to moisture and oxygen, helping slow corrosion. Left exposed, rust can spread beneath surrounding paint, causing more peeling and pitting. Over time, severe corrosion can weaken components. Painting over loose rust does not solve the underlying problem,” explains Sharkey.

    Moisture from ice and snow can cause significant damage to concrete because it is a highly porous material. When snow melts on walkways, driveways, or patios, the concrete absorbs the water. Subsequent freezing temperatures cause that internal water to expand, which leads to surface flaking, scaling, and deep cracking.

    Industry observers note that unlike surface coatings, penetrating sealers chemically bond inside concrete pores. They create an invisible, breathable hydrophobic barrier that prevents liquid water from sinking into the stone, while still allowing internal vapor to escape.

    Sources indicate that sharkey notes that “for compatible, absorbent concrete steps, walkways, or patios, a penetrating sealer rated for exterior concrete and freeze-thaw exposure can reduce water absorption. Confirm compatibility with any existing treatment and follow the preparation instructions.”.

    Reducing water and deicing-salt penetration helps protect against winter deterioration. However, just keep in mind that a sealer is preventive maintenance; it does not repair cracks, failing concrete, or drainage problems.

    According to recent reports, gas-powered snow blowers use 4-cycle engine oil, a type of oil for snow blower engines that uses separate tanks for gas and oil, much like car engines. The gas fuels the engine, while the oil lubricates it.

    Smaller engines, such as those on chainsaws, have 2-cycle engines. This type of small engine uses an oil and gas mixture that goes into one tank. Don’t use 2-cycle engine oil in a snow blower, as it will not properly lubricate the engine and will damage it. The motors on electric snow blowers don’t require engine oil.

    Identifying the right type of engine oil is easy. The oil container has “4-cycle” or “2-cycle” clearly printed on the label. Although some 4-cycle engine oils are labeled for “small engines,” they are actually the same oil commonly used in cars and trucks.

    Viscosity refers to the thickness of the oil. Higher viscosity oil is better at protecting and lubricating engines at high temperatures and peak load (high RPMs). Oil with a low viscosity remains thinner at lower temperatures, promoting better flow through the engine, making it easier to start and more efficient to run.

    In a recent development, viscosity is based on a scale created by SAE International, formerly known as the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE). Motor oil has two viscosity ratings:.

    Since snow blowers operate exclusively in cold weather, they typically use SAE 5W-30 weight oil, which ensures the engine will start at low temperatures. Make sure to check the maintenance section of your operating manual for the proper snow blower oil weight for your machine.

    In a recent development, following a few energy-saving strategies when setting the temperature on your thermostat can make a big difference in winter. According to the U.S. Department of Energy, it’s possible to save 10 percent a year on energy bills by being conservative with thermostat settings year-round.

    Industry observers note that we consulted an HVAC expert about thermostat-setting strategies during the coldest months of the year, and how we can save on energy costs. Here’s what he said.

    “I prefer setting the thermostat to around 68 degrees Fahrenheit (20 degrees Celsius) during the day. This temperature strikes a balance between comfort and energy efficiency,” states Josh Mitchell, HVAC technician and founder of Air Conditioner Lab. “At night, lowering it to about 65 degrees Fahrenheit (18 degrees Celsius) is comfortable for sleeping and helps save on heating costs.”.

    According to the Department of Energy, setting your thermostat to the lowest comfortable temperature, which is typically 68 degrees Fahrenheit in the winter, helps slow down heat loss for homes with a regular furnace or baseboard heating system. However, that’s not the case for homes with heat pumps. Dialing down the thermostat too much can make a heat pump less efficient.

    In a recent development, everyone has a different comfort zone when it comes to temperatures. Just because 68 degrees can be an ideal temperature for a house in terms of reducing energy consumption doesn’t mean it’s right for everyone. Some people may prefer to set the thermostat slightly higher, at 70 degrees, and that’s okay.

    The  Amazon Smart Thermostat uses Alexa to adjust the thermostat based on whether it thinks you’re home. Read the review.

    It’s important to install a thermostat in the right location to prevent inaccurate temperature readings. Called ‘ghost readings,’ a thermostat may be triggered to run unnecessarily if placed near drafts, sunlight, and doorways. If air flow near the thermostat is blocked by furniture, also may not run effectively.

    Mitchell says that the best place to locate a thermostat is on an interior wall that experiences the natural air flow in the home and is away from direct sunlight, drafts, doorways, and windows.

    Sources indicate that your body requires time to adapt to slightly cooler temperatures. So there’s no need to (literally) go cold turkey when cooler outdoor temps arrive. Lower the temperature gradually, so you have time to adjust to being a little chilly. Until you acclimate, wear layers, don warm socks, and have a snuggly blanket on hand.

    According to recent reports, regardless of how low you set the thermostat, you won’t save on your heating bill if your furnace or heating system works inefficiently. Make sure to do the following:.

    It has been revealed that “Setting the thermostat too high in winter can lead to excessive energy consumption and higher utility bills,” Mitchell explains. “Conversely, setting it too low might not provide adequate comfort and could even risk pipes freezing. The key is to find a balanced setting that ensures comfort without overburdening your heating system.”.

    RELATED: Can Your Utility Firm Control Your Home’s Thermostat?

    Consider investing in a programmable thermostat that’ll automatically adjust the temperature for you. Programmable thermostats are ideal for people with consistent schedules.

    “I’m a strong advocate for smart thermostats,” Mitchell states. “They offer advanced features like learning your schedule, remote control via a smartphone app, and energy usage reports, which not only enhances energy efficiency but also contributes to a more comfortable living environment.”.

    In a recent development, if your day-to-day routine is a bit more haphazard than a regular 9 to 5, consider a smart thermostat. Helpful features of some smart thermostats include settings that automatically detect your absence and lower the thermostat temperature while you’re gone. Some units can adjust the indoor temperature based on weather data.

    “The ability to monitor and adjust your home’s temperature settings from anywhere can lead to cost savings and reduce your carbon footprint,” Mitchell explains.

    Unless you work from home, turning the thermostat down during the workday can mean substantial savings on your energy bill. If you have pets, of course, you’ll want to set the thermostat to a temperature that will keep them comfortable while you’re gone. Still, the exact comfort zone will vary depending on the kind of pet and the animal’s size.

    Another good opportunity to lower your thermostat is while you sleep. After all, research suggests that most people sleep poorly in overly warm conditions.

    15 Things You Should Never Burn in the Fireplace

    📅 12 Jan 2024 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
    • It has been revealed that thanks to modern heating technologies, homeowners today no longer have to rely on fire for heat.
    • Be smart, however, about what you toss on the fire; some combustibles can cause immediate danger, such as serious respiratory reactions, or contribute to long-term problems, such as creosote buildup, which can lead to chimney fires.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    It has been revealed that thanks to modern heating technologies, homeowners today no longer have to rely on fire for heat. But that doesn’t mean a crackling fire in the fireplace isn’t a wonderful antidote to a cold evening, and more and more are embracing this cozy heating method. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the number of fireplaces built in single-family homes has been steadily increasing over the last decade. And Verified Market Research says the wood stoves market size was valued at $8.35 billion in 2025 and projected to reach $14.89 billion by 2033.

    Be smart, however, about what you toss on the fire; some combustibles can cause immediate danger, such as serious respiratory reactions, or contribute to long-term problems, such as creosote buildup, which can lead to chimney fires.

    It has been revealed that when you burn coated or pressure-treated wood, toxic chemicals can be released into the air you breathe. For example, wood treated to withstand rot or insects used to contain a form of arsenic, and painted, stained, or varnished woods contain other chemicals—and all these chemicals create toxic fumes when burned. Nix on plywood, too, because adhesives applied during manufacturing release toxic fumes when burned.

    Sources indicate that treated lumber often has a stamp or a tag on it to indicate it’s been altered, but of course, those might be missing from scrap lumber. Look for a green or blue tint or an oily feel—or simply err on the side of caution and refrain from burning any lumber in your fireplace.

    Industry observers note that small recyclables are often used to start a roaring fire because they usually catch fire quickly. The next time you need to get a fire going, however, don’t use cardboard, which is often treated with chemicals, dyes, and glues. Additionally, burning cardboard bits can often float out of the fire and onto your carpet or furniture. Instead, use approved fire starters, available from camping-supply stores, or small splinters of wood, chipped with an ax from your stock of seasoned firewood.

    Odorless, nontoxic, and eco-friendly, Superior Trading’s fire starters are made of food-grade wax and wood shavings. Read the review.

    According to recent reports, never use lighter fluid, charcoal starter fluid, or any other type of accelerant to start a fire in a fireplace. These products should not be used to fuel an indoor fire, in part because they often contain methanol and petroleum-based chemicals that produce toxic fumes. In addition, the use of accelerants creates an extra-hot fire that can damage your chimney liner.

    RELATED: The Best Fire Logs for Long-Lasting Ambience, Tested.

    Recent findings suggest that the inks used to create colorful magazine layouts contain chemical pigments that release toxic fumes when burned. You may instead use a couple of sheets (not more) of plain black-and-white newspaper, rolled tightly and placed beneath small bits of wood kindling, but don’t toss magazines, gift wrap, or coupon inserts into the fireplace. Not only do these items create unwanted fumes, but bits of burning paper can float up and out of an uncapped chimney, putting your roof and nearby structures at risk of fire.

    RELATED: The Best Creosote Removers to Keep Your Chimney Clean.

    Recent findings suggest that the best thing you can do to make sure your firewood is always fireplace-ready is to keep it dry. For starters, dry wood is easier to light than damp wood. Even more notable, the moisture in wet firewood makes it smoke and leads to rapid creosote buildup in the chimney liner. In fact, creosote buildup is a leading cause of chimney fires. While you can’t completely avoid creosote, you can reduce the risk of buildup by burning only dry firewood and having your chimney cleaned annually.

    It has been revealed that this creosote remover dissolves first- and second-degree creosote in your chimney, turning it into ash. Read our full review.

    You wouldn’t intentionally roll around in a patch of poison oak, but you’ll put your whole family at risk if you burn the woody vines from poison sumac, poison ivy, or plants that contain urushiol, a toxic irritant that causes rashes on contact. In winter, when plants lose their leaves, it can be difficult to tell if you’re gathering harmless vines or poisonous ones, so take precautions by avoiding anything you can’t identify. The reason? Fumes from burning plants that contain urushiol can trigger serious allergic respiratory reactions.

    Evergreen trees, such as pine, spruce, and cedar (yes, even your old Christmas tree), contain resins that catch fire quickly and produce a hot flame. While this might sound good, these trees burn so fast that the fire will fizzle out quickly, and their high resin content can leave heavy creosote deposits in your chimney, which can over time lead to chimney fires.

    Recent findings suggest that finding a way to repurpose wood shipping pallets is a great idea—just don’t burn them. Discarded shipping pallets are popular materials for resourceful DIYers and crafters, but many pallets have been treated with the chemical pesticide methyl bromide to prevent the spread of the emerald ash borer, a beetle that wreaks havoc on living ash trees. Never burn a pallet that bears the stamp “MB,” which indicates that it has been treated with chemicals. Even if you don’t see a stamp, it’s probably safest to avoid burning pallets altogether.

    If you’ve ever attended a beach party where driftwood was burned, you probably marveled at the beautiful lavender-blue flames. Those colorful flames are produced by metal salts that the wood absorbed while it was adrift, and, unfortunately, the fumes from those flames are toxic. Many seaside communities have banned the burning of driftwood for just that reason, so follow their lead and don’t burn wood that you’ve gathered on the beach in your fireplace.

    Most consumer products contain chemicals that produce hazardous fumes when burned. What’s worse? Some of the most toxic trash items contain plastic, which releases a category of toxins known as dioxins. Inhaling dioxins increases the risk of respiratory ailments, headaches, internal organ damage, and even cancer. And as we noted before, lightweight bits of burning material can float out of the fireplace and onto surfaces in your home—not good!

    Starting a fire at home with a base of dried leaves might seem like a good way to put fallen leaves to use, but it’s not. First, leaves burn very swiftly and hot. This sudden and extreme change in temperature can crack chimney flues and masonry, which is why it’s best to get your fireplace going with a chimney starter instead. Wet leaves will do the opposite, burning slowly while smoldering and creating a ton of smoke. That smoke generates creosote buildup, which can cause chimney fires.

    Sources indicate that many folks like adding scents to their fireplace, opting for the fresh aromas of oranges, lemons, apples, and the like. The problem is that fresh, moist fruit peels will smolder in a fire, and lead to abundant smoke and creosote buildup. A better course of action is to dry your fruit peels at a low temperature in the oven, and then toss them on your fire. You’ll still get a fresh scent, but not the moisture.

    RELATED: 20 Crazy Cleaning Tips That Actually Work.

    Believe it or not, decades ago magazine ads actually encouraged homeowners to burn batteries in their fireplaces because burning zinc was believed to prevent creosote formation (burning batteries also resulted in a rainbow of beautiful colors). While that might’ve been true, modern batteries will explode under extreme heat and potentially cause severe chemical burns. Beyond the potential burns, fumes from burning chemicals are also poisonous. Instead, it’s best to dispose of batteries the right way.

    Recent findings suggest that it might seem like a good idea to throw old T-shirts, rags, and other fabric in a fireplace to start a fire, but you’d be wrong. Cloth and clothing will create a nasty smell as well as a ton of smoke as it smolders. That smoke will coat the inside of the chimney with creosote, which can cause chimney fires. A better course of action is to pack those old shirts up and drop them off at the local homeless shelter or SPCA.

    RELATED: How to Get Your Fireplace Ready for Winter.

    In a recent development, anyone who’s seen the red-hot glow in the bottom of a charcoal grill knows that charcoal can create a ton of heat. It also produces carbon monoxide, which isn’t as dangerous in the open air as it is indoors. However, if there’s too much draft the charcoal can burn twice as hot as wood, which could damage the chimney or flue. For that reason, charcoal’s best left for summer grilling outdoors.

    While the fireplace is not the best disposal solution for most household trash, there are a few items you can safely dispose of in the fireplace rather than sending them to the landfill:.

    The Right Types of Christmas Lights for Indoor and Outdoor Holiday Displays
